contributions.headingText: Supratentorial ependymoma, YAP1 fusion–positive, is a circumscribed supratentorial glioma with a YAP1 fusion gene, focally demonstrating pseudorosettes or ependymal rosettes and comprising uniform small cells with round nuclei embedded in a fibrillary matrix. In most of these supratentorial ependymomas, YAP1 is fused with MAMLD1.
2A00.0Y & XH1511 Other specified gliomas of brain & Ependymoma, NOS
Most YAP1 fusion–positive tumours are located within or adjacent to the lateral ventricle.

YAP1 fusion–positive supratentorial ependymomas are often large by the time of presentation. Clinical features include symptoms and signs of raised intracranial pressure, as well as focal neurological deficits or seizures.

Imaging

Neuroimaging shows that tumours have sharp margins and prominent cystic components. They are mostly isointense on T1- and T2-weighted images. Contrast enhancement of solid tumour components is heterogeneous. Peritumoural oedema is variable {30246434}.

YAP1 fusion–positive ependymomas are uncommon and appear to be restricted to young children. In paediatric cohorts, they account for 6–7.4% of supratentorial ependymomas. The M:F ratio is 0.3:1 {25965575; 30053291; 30246434; 30325077; 30976811}.
Data suggest that YAP1 fusion–positive ependymomas derive from PAX6-positive radial glial neural stem cells {31477715; 32404936}.

Genomic fusions of the YAP1 gene with MAMLD1 or other partner genes appear to be the principal oncogenic driver of the disease. Functional genomic analyses suggest that YAP1::MAMLD1 fusions function as an oncogenic driver through the recruitment of nuclear factor I (NFI) and TEA domain (TEAD) family members {31477715; 32404936}.
Ependymomas with a YAP1 fusion have macroscopic appearances similar to those of other supratentorial ependymomas. They are circumscribed and focally haemorrhagic, with a soft consistency.

Like other ependymal tumours, YAP1-fused supratentorial ependymomas are demarcated from adjacent brain. They are composed of relatively uniform cells with small to medium-sized round or angulated nuclei. Ependymal rosettes are present in some tumours. Clear cell, papillary, or tanycytic phenotypes have not been recorded. Mitotic activity is highly variable. In most cases, the fibrillary matrix contains PAS-positive eosinophilic granular bodies {30246434}. Frequent findings are vascular endothelial proliferation, dystrophic calcification, and necrosis.

Immunophenotype

Supratentorial ependymomas with a YAP1 fusion show widespread and strong immunoreactivity for EMA {30246434}. There is no expression of L1CAM, and tumour cell nuclei are negative for p65 (RELA).

Grading

YAP1-fused supratentorial ependymomas show variable degrees of anaplasia, and such information should be included in an integrated diagnosis {24990071}.

Cytological preparations generally show uniform cells with round nuclei and sparse delicate cytoplasmic processes. Nuclear pleomorphism is generally mild, but it is exaggerated in the rare giant cell phenotype {16389948; 22808300}.

Molecular testing for YAP1 fusions includes several sequencing strategies and interphase FISH {29354850; 30514397; 31679042}. DNA methylation–based classification can complement tests directed towards identification of the fusion.

Although often large at presentation and predominantly occurring in young children, ependymomas with a YAP1 fusion carry a prognosis in retrospectively studied cohorts that appears to be favourable when compared with that of other supratentorial ependymal tumour types {30246434; 30325077; 30976811}. Molecular markers or clinical characteristics further defining prognosis in these tumours are currently unknown.
